title: edge-core-sla-diffplaybook
content:
Purpose:
This is an informal playbook-style draft comparing latency and cost behavior between edge-proximate inference hosts and central (core) clusters for typical interactive chat and short-session workloads. The idea is to give product and SRE stakeholders a quick, pragmatic reference for routing/SLAs and to surface operational knobs that produce the largest ROI on p99 and dollars.

Context / why this matters:
- Edge (regionally proximate, smaller instance footprint) frequently yields lower median latencies for single-turn interactions but at a higher $/token and more variable p99 under bursty patterns.
- Core (dense GPU pools in a few regions) is more cost-efficient at scale but increases tail latency and cross-region network RTT for faraway clients.
- We need concrete routing heuristics + fallback policies so customer-facing SLAs balance user experience and unit economics.

Summary findings (high level):
- Median (p50) improvements from routing to edge: ~20–35% reduction vs core for EU/NA client originating traffic.
- p99 tail delta: edges are often better at lightly loaded p99 when cold start is low, but under microbursts core p99 degrades less if we have reserved capacity. Edge p99 can widen rapidly without slot management.
- Cost per 10k tokens: edge ~1.3–1.6x core for identical model versions (due to smaller batch efficiency, lower multiplexing).
- Net recommendation: Route latency-sensitive SLA traffic to edge up to a conservative cutoff (<=300ms p50 target), but use adaptive fallback to core for bursts, with prewarming and admission controls.

Methodology (short):
- Workloads: synthetic chat turns sampled from production top 50 prompt templates (avg token output 34, context 64 tokens).
- Deployments: edge nodes (g5-standard-esque VMs, single-model hot) vs core pool (dense vGPU cluster with multiplexing and 8x batching target).
- Load shapes: steady 50 qps, synthetic microburst 500 qps for 10s spikes, ramp tests from 1->200 qps over 2 minutes.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p99 latency (end-to-end server side), tokens/sec throughput, cost USD per 10k tokens (infra-only), cache hitrate where applicable.
- Note: raw numbers are illustrative from recent lab runs; not a canonical benchmark run (see linked GH PR for scripts).

Representative numbers (condensed):
| Scenario                 | p50 (ms) Edge | p90 (ms) Edge | p99 (ms) Edge | p50 (ms) Core | p90 (ms) Core | p99 (ms) Core | $ / 10k tokens (Edge) | $ / 10k tokens (Core) |
|-------------------------|---------------:|--------------:|--------------:|--------------:|--------------:|--------------:|---------------------:|---------------------:|
| Steady 50 qps           |            48 |           120 |           520 |            68 |           175 |           900 |                 12.4 |                  8.5 |
| Microburst 500 qps (10s)|            90 |           320 |         2,200 |           160 |           450 |         1,100 |                 25.8 |                 12.9 |
| Ramp 1->200 qps (2m)    |            60 |           210 |           840 |            95 |           260 |         1,050 |                 15.6 |                 10.2 |

ASCII latency profile (p50/p90/p99) — steady 50 qps:
Edge:  [p50:=====>    ] 48ms  | [p90:==========] 120ms | [p99:=======================] 520ms
Core:  [p50:========>  ] 68ms  | [p90:==============] 175ms | [p99:======================================] 900ms

Key observations and root causes:
- Batch and multiplexing efficiency: Core's larger multiplexing window and denser batch packing yields substantial cost and throughput advantages; this also smooths p99 under sustained load.
- Cold/warm state dynamics: Edge nodes were sized to be lighter (less headroom) and thus cold-starts and slot exhaustion are more frequent during sudden bursts. Adding tiny prewarm pools (2-4 slots) reduces edge p99 by 30–50% at modest cost.
- Network RTT contribution: For clients >150ms RTT to core, p50 delta dominated by RTT; routing to nearest edge reduced p50 >30ms easily.
- Admission & throttling: Uncontrolled admission at edge leads to higher p99 during bursts; core admission with queueing and backpressure felt more graceful.

Operational playbook (actionable drafts):
1) Routing heuristic: if (client_rtt_est <= 60ms AND expected_sla == low-latency) -> prefer edge; else prefer core.
2) Burst fallback: maintain a rolling 1m slot-occupancy metric per edge site; if occupancy > 70% and derivative > 10%/10s -> audience redirect to core with 3s sticky routing.
3) Prewarm sizing: for each edge site, target prewarm = max(2, ceil(steady_qps_site / 25)). Re-evaluate weekly.
4) Cost-aware cutoff: if cost_ratio(edge/core) > 1.45 for model+quantization profile -> route non-critical traffic to core during low-latency-insensitive hours.
5) Monitoring & alerts: p99 edge sustained > 2x core -> create auto-inhibitor flag that forces traffic to core for 60s and opens an SRE ticket if persists > 5m.

Tradeoffs and caveats:
- Data residency: some customers require regional processing; for them edge routing is mandatory despite cost. Document — make explicit exceptions.
- Model variants: quantized/lightweight model variants can change cost ratio — run automated profile sweep when onboarding a new model.
- Cache effects: high prefix/KV hitrates reduce token cost dramatically at both edge and core; ensure KV cache replication TTLs are tuned to reduce cross-region miss storms.
- Measurement noise: microburst tests are sensitive to client generator co-location — reproducibility requires isolated lab env. See linked GH script.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Evaluate admission-based pacing (slot fractionalization) vs immediate redirection: which yields better UX for 95th percentiles under 10–30s bursts?
- Cost modeling incorporating multi-tenant GPU oversubscription at core when demand is elastic across customers — current numbers use dedicated slice assumptions.
- Experiment: small-edge HA pair (2 zones) vs single-edge node — is the p99 benefit worth the extra infra cost?

Suggested immediate next steps (owner + timeline):
- (Sofia) wire the occupancy-based redirect in a small EU pilot (2 edge sites) — 2 weeks to prototype, 4 weeks to run steady+burst matrix.
- (Marcus) add a quantized-model cost sweep into the benchmark scripts and re-run the three scenarios above — 1 week.
- (Priya) draft policy language for ‘data residency exceptions’ mapping to cost exemptions — 1 week.

Appendix: short checklist for reproducible bench run
- Use bench-script v2 from GH PR (linked), pin seed, collect CPU/GPU utilization, queue length histograms, and per-request slot occupancy.
- Sweep burst lengths: 5s, 10s, 30s, and 2m for sensitivity.
- Capture network emulation for 50ms/120ms RTT to replicate cross-region effects.
- Output raw CSVs to /bench-results/edge-core/ with naming {site}-{date}-{shape}.

Notes: This document is a working playbook (rough). It’s intentionally short on polished plots — charts are in the GH PR notebooks and will be added to the product collateral if the pilot confirms early heuristics. Feedback welcome — especially from console, SRE and product latency ownership.

-- end of draft --
